extracted.intended_audience: researchers, journal editors, publishers, and policy-makers interested in peer review reform and Open Science
extracted.subtask_description: A systematic-review style synthesis defining and assessing multiple traits of Open Peer Review (OPR), mapping each trait's aims, benefits, drawbacks, evidence, and example implementations to inform design and evaluation of peer review models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open identities
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors and reviewers are aware of each other’s identity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposed benefits: increases accountability, enables credit for reviewers, makes conflicts of interest more apparent, and may motivate reviewers to invest more care. Opposing concerns: signing may lead to poorer reviews as reviewers temper criticism to avoid offence; may discourage review participation. Evidence: mixed and limited — studies to date (largely in medicine) show no clear effect on review quality; reviewer identification of authors is often possible (26–46% identification rates). Discipline differences: more common / central in SSH definitions of OPR than in STEM. Examples/discussion: arguments for fairness and accountability (van Rooyen et al., Bloom 2017), but more research needed as existing studies are limited in disciplinary scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Review reports (either full reports or summaries) are published alongside the relevant article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Benefits: makes otherwise invisible scholarly information available for reuse, increases transparency and accountability, provides additional quality assurance by exposing reviews to community scrutiny, can incentivize and reward reviewers by making reviews part of scholarly record (e.g., via ORCID/Publons), and serves as a pedagogical guide for early-career reviewers (tone, length, formulation of criticisms). Drawbacks/effects observed: higher reviewer refusal rates and increased time to write reviews in some studies, with no clear concomitant improvement in quality (van Rooyen et al., 2010). Evidence: mixed and limited; attitudes in some surveys are positive (Nicholson & Alperin, 2016).

rubrics_metrics.name: Open participation
rubrics_metrics.description: The wider community is able to contribute to the review process (crowdsourced/community/public review).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: expands reviewer pool beyond editor-invited peers to include related disciplines, interdisciplines, industry, patients, and public stakeholders; may reduce editorial bias and closed networks. Potential benefits: increases number and diversity of reviewers, possibly improving accuracy if enough qualified public reviewers participate (modeling suggests >50 reader-reviewers needed in one model). Criticisms and limitations: concerns about commenters' qualifications and incentives, low participation rates in practice (Nature trial: 5% of authors, many papers received no comments; ACP: ~1 in 5 papers commented), and many comments being insubstantial. Conclusion: likely a useful complement to invited review but unlikely to fully replace it; discipline differences (more central in SSH where narrative and argument assessment is more transferable).

rubrics_metrics.name: Open interaction
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct reciprocal discussion between reviewers, and/or between author(s) and reviewers, is allowed and encouraged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intended benefits: improves communication, fosters collaborative discourse to improve manuscripts, may produce more accurate reviewing through cooperation. Examples: EMBO "cross-peer review" where referees comment on each other's reports; eLife online consultation to produce a single summary; Frontiers' interactive collaboration stage uniting authors, reviewers and editors. Evidence: largely anecdotal and scarce; one laboratory study suggests improved reviewing accuracy with interaction (Leek et al., 2011). Potential trade-offs: more back-and-forth and editorial mediation may increase review time and cost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open pre-review manuscripts
rubrics_metrics.description: Manuscripts are made immediately openly accessible (e.g., via preprint servers) in advance of any formal peer review procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Benefits: allows authors to assert priority, increases visibility and early dissemination, enables open participation and real-time comment incorporation, may improve initial submission quality. Implementation examples: arXiv, bioRxiv, Zenodo, Figshare, PeerJ Preprints, overlay journals (Discrete Analysis), and publisher-hosted preprints. Models: preprints used alongside traditional review, or overlay services add review functions to repositories (e.g., F1000Research, Open Peer Review Module for repositories). Potential drawbacks: none inherent noted, but complements rather than eliminates traditional peer review in many models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open final-version commenting
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewing or commenting on the final 'version of record' publications (post-publication commentary).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: the internet enables expansive reader feedback beyond formal letters; post-publication commentary can be continuous and allow science to self-correct. Benefits: ongoing reputation evolution, corrections/retractions initiated by community scrutiny, platforms (e.g., PubPeer) have surfaced significant issues missed in pre-publication review. Usage: many journals offer comment facilities but they are often little used; post-publication comments also occur on blogs and social networks. Examples: PubPeer's critique of STAP paper; Living Reviews journals that update invited articles. Limitations: uptake variable; decoupling from journals means peer review can be dispersed across platforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open platforms (decoupled review)
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review is facilitated by a different organizational entity than the venue of publication (portable or independent review services).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Models and aims: services invite manuscripts, organize reviews, and return reports that journals may use (portable reviews) to reduce duplication of effort across submissions. Examples: RUBRIQ (pays reviewers), Peerage of Science, Axios Review (forwarded manuscript and reviews to target journal), Publons (collects/validates review records), overlay journals using preprint archives (Discrete Analysis). Variants: paid reviewer models, community models with incentives (discounts), overlay journals that perform only review while hosting content on archives. Benefits: reduce inefficiencies from repeated reviews at multiple journals, enable transferable review records, and support alternative incentive structures. Challenges: sustainability and uptake vary by model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blinding and anonymity models
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditional reviewer/author anonymity models (single-blind, where reviewers know authors but authors do not know reviewers; double-blind, where both remain anonymous) and their intended purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: author anonymity aims to reduce publication biases (against gendered names, less prestigious institutions, non-English regions); reviewer anonymity aims to protect candid feedback from reprisals. Evidence: multiple studies failed to show that blinding increases review quality (e.g., Godlee et al., 1998; Fisher et al., 1994), and author anonymity is only partially effective because reviewers can identify authors in a substantial fraction of cases (26–46%). Trade-offs: removing anonymity may increase accountability and credit but may discourage frank criticism and change reviewer willingness to participate. Disciplinary variation: double-blind more common in Arts, Humanities, Social Sciences; single-blind most common overall.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliability and consistency (evaluation dimension)
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the peer review model reduce unreliability and inconsistency across reviews?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theorized effects: open identities and open reports may improve thoroughness by increasing reviewer accountability; open participation and final-version commenting could improve reliability by increasing reviewer numbers and perspectives; open interaction might improve accuracy through cooperation. Evidence: limited and mixed — some models theoretical or supported by small studies or modeling; open participation often fails to attract sufficient high-quality engagement in practice. Evaluation should consider actual reviewer numbers, reviewer qualifications, and empirical measures of inter-review agreement or error detection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delay and expense (timeliness & cost)
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the peer review model reduce delays to dissemination and decrease the cost of the review/publication process?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open pre-review manuscripts sharply reduce time to public availability. Open platforms can reduce duplicated review cycles by making reviews portable. Conversely, open identities and open reports may increase reviewer refusal rates and time spent on reviews, and open interaction may increase back-and-forth leading to longer review times. Empirical assessment should measure time-to-publication, reviewer recruitment costs, and total reviewer-hours.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accountability and risks of subversion
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the model increase accountability and transparency, while avoiding subversion or conflicts of interest?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open identities and open reports increase transparency and make conflicts more apparent, potentially improving accountability. However, openness may discourage strong criticism or invite engagement by conflicted parties if open participation is unchecked. Evaluation should examine conflict-of-interest disclosure, incidence of tempered criticism, and whether openness exposes or mitigates manipulative behaviors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social and publication biases
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the model reduce or exacerbate biases related to author identity, institution, region, gender, or status?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open reports add transparency to editorial decisions; open identities remove anonymity protections intended to counteract biases but evidence that anonymity prevents bias is weak. Open participation could reduce elite/closed-network biases by widening reviewer pools, but could also enable biased engagement or conflicts if not curated. Assessment should use empirical measures of acceptance rates across demographic/institutional groups under different models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incentives for reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the model provide recognition, credit, or other incentives that increase reviewer participation and quality?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open reports linked to open identities and platforms (e.g., Publons, ORCID integration) can make reviewing visible and countable for career advancement. Open participation lets reviewers choose work they find relevant. However, some open models correlate with lower willingness to review (higher refusal rates) and mixed effects on time invested. Evaluation should track reviewer recruitment/retention, reported motivations, and integration of review activity into research assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wastefulness and reuse of reviewer effort
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the model reduce waste from redundant reviews and make reviewer contributions reusable?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open reports and open platforms can make reviews available for reuse (e.g., portable review transfers, published reports), and provide guidance material for early-career reviewers. Portable review services and overlay journals aim to reduce duplicate review cycles when manuscripts are submitted to multiple journals. Evaluation should measure number of repeated review cycles per manuscript, reuse/adoption rates of portable reviews, and whether published reports are reused or cited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence-base and need for empirical evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Quality of empirical evidence supporting claims about the effects of different OPR traits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper repeatedly notes that the evidence base is limited, often discipline-specific (many studies in medicine), and sometimes anecdotal or from small surveys/experiments. The author emphasizes a pressing need for more empirical research to evaluate the efficacy of differing OPR traits. Any implementation or policy decision should be accompanied by robust empirical evaluation (recruitment metrics, quality measures, time/cost measures, disciplinary variation).
